newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ bills shine at close in face of weaker TWI.
newsitem.headline: NZ bills shine at close in face of weaker TWI.

text.p: Figures in brackets compare against previous day's close
FUTURES PHYSICAL YIELD (PCT)
90-DAY BILLS (JUN) 92.99 (PREV 92.92) 90-DAYS 6.78 (PREV 6.86)
OVERNIGHT CASH 6.00 PCT (PREV 6.00) US 5-YR 6.51 (PREV 6.55)
* NZ bank bills finish stronger despite slip in TWI
* Volumes reasonable, bonds also bid
* Market awaits Tuesday's employment data
The New Zealand money market caught up with the rest of the yield curve's bid tone at Monday's close following a steady open.
The key 90-day bank bills ended eight basis points stronger at 6.78 percent, while the front futures contract was up seven at 92.99 with nearly 3,000 contracts traded.
"Despite the TWI coming off this afternoon the bills have still held in really well," an Auckland dealer said. The TWI was finishing at 68.48, compared to its 68.54 close on Friday.

Dealers said that following comments from Reserve Bank of New Zealand governor Don Brash last week, the market generally believed Brash would accommodate easier monetary conditions, even though he did not explicitly say so.

This meant traders were happy to keep rates low, but it also had the disadvantage of undermining monetary conditions indices (MCI) based on the RBNZ's March economic projections, which assumed a TWI at 68.0 and 90-day bank bills at 7.5 percent.
One dealer said there was a guessing game going on ahead of the central bank's June monetary policy statement, as the market tried to ascertain where the new RBNZ-approved MCI line might lie.
"Most people are almost certain there's no way he (Brash) will tighten come the June statement, and it's more likely, if he's going to do anything, that he will probably ease.

"So I think we'll stay reasonably well bid, assuming the Kiwi doesn't fall out of bed, right through until that statement, as long as the data continues to come out either soft or on expectations," the dealer said.
March quarter Household Labour Force data is due on Tuesday at 10.45 a.m. (2245 GMT).

Economists expect on average unemployment to rise to 6.2 percent from 5.9 percent in the December quarter, and quarterly employment growth of around 0.3 percent (versus -0.5 percent in December quarter).

Meanwhile, bonds retained their bid tone from early trade, after U.S. Treasuries rallied on the announcement of a balanced budget accord, and on the back of a growing expectation that the Federal Reserve will not tighten monetary policy further at its next meeting on May 20.
-- Catherine McCaw, Wellington newsroom (64 4) 471 4275
